title: Judge Loop and One-Minute Segments
eyebrow: house-rules · fix proposal · nothing built yet
approval: Design approved: judge blocking fix and one-minute segments

short.lead: The end-of-reply judge blocked 12 times in a row, even when the model had tried three different ways. Its criteria are a single sentence, and the model is never shown what a passing reply looks like. I propose keeping the judge and tuning it. A second part makes every job that involves waiting, not only tests, run as independent segments of at most a minute that each print their own result, so a failure shows up early and nobody waits 20 minutes for one output.
short.hint: Tap a step to see what it changes. The choices at the end are yours.

changes: new
What exists today
Three checks run each time Claude finishes a reply (the Stop event), and they do not know about each other.

The judge is the Stop entry of type prompt in hooks.json. Its criteria are one sentence: flag a claim that something cannot be done, verified, tested or reached unless the reply lists three different methods. It never says what counts as a different method. It sees only the last reply, not the tool calls. When it blocks, it does not say which rule the reply failed. So a model that really ran three checks can still fail, as happened to me four times in this session: the judge counted three ways of reading the same output as one method, and it flagged plain notes about what had not been checked. It also keeps no count of how many times it has blocked. The scripted record check (scripts/house_rules/core.py, roadblock_check) already groups methods into classes and stops after two blocks; the goal check stops after six blocks, using its own separate counter. I did not find the transcript of your 12-block session, so I could not reproduce the 12 blocks.
A judge with a one-sentence rule and no count.
The same judge with four written criteria and a shared cap.
A model that did the work passes, and a model that did not is told exactly what is missing.
adapt
Write the judge's criteria down
Four numbered criteria, with the same wording used in the judge, in the block message and in the rules.

The criteria live once, in rules/detail/roadblocks.md. C1, what triggers a block: the reply claims something is missing, unreachable or impossible, and that claim stops the task. A note about what was not checked is not a trigger if it is written as an Unverified line. C2, what passes: three attempts in this turn. Each must be aimed at the thing claimed to be missing, and each must come from a different method class. The classes are: existence check, disk search, package database, running it, asking the environment, or another source such as CI (automated builds), git history or docs. Reading one output three ways counts as one method. C3, proof: the attempts must appear in the real tool calls, and the judge is shown those calls. C4, the ways out: a "No other method" line with its reason; a "NEEDS YOU" line for a licence, login, purchase or destructive step; or an Unverified line. When it blocks, the judge returns the criterion the reply failed and the exact line to add.
One sentence, and the model has to guess what passes.
Four criteria, one source, quoted in every block.
The model always knows what to fix.
adapt
One shared cap
The judge, the record check and the goal check share one counter that allows two blocks per user message.

After two blocks the reply goes out with a visible warning. The counter resets only if the model made at least one real tool call after the last block. So a model that keeps working is checked again, and a model that only rewords its reply is not blocked a third time. A prompt hook (a hook that asks the model a question) cannot keep a count, so the first choice below decides where the judge runs.
Two counters with caps 2 and 6.
One counter with cap 2.
The worst case is two blocks, not twelve.
adapt
Fewer false alarms
Stop treating ordinary phrases as roadblocks.

The phrase "next step" is removed from the list of stall phrases, because the house rules themselves tell every reply to end with one next step. The list of claim phrases drops the bare phrases "could not", "unable to" and "I can't". It keeps phrases about a missing tool, machine or access. The judge no longer flags a plain Unverified note, which the evidence rule requires. A reply with a NEEDS YOU line is also exempt from the goal check.
The stall-phrase list (_STALL_RE) and the claim-phrase list (_ROADBLOCK_RE) in core.py.
Narrower lists, and NEEDS YOU exempts both checks.
Normal status replies pass.
new
The passing reply, spelled out
Each block message includes the exact lines the model can copy into its reply.

Each block quotes the claim it matched, names the failed criterion (C1 to C4), says which method classes the record already covers, lists the ones still missing, and gives a concrete command for each missing one, says how many blocks remain, and shows the five accepted forms. They are: a Roadblock record of three numbered methods with what each returned; a "No other method" line with the reason; a "NEEDS YOU" line; an "Unverified" line (what was not checked, why, and the command that would check it); or a "Goal status" line. The record is still checked against the real failed tool calls, so invented methods do not pass. The same forms are written into rules/detail/roadblocks.md so the model knows them before it is blocked.
Messages say only to try three methods.
Messages carry a copyable accepted reply.
The model can always find the way out.
new
What exists today for waits and tests
The rules already limit waits, but allow 20-minute jobs, and only the tests have a design for being split into separate parts.

Waits: rules/waits.json limits a foreground command to 60 seconds. It allows deadlines of 600 seconds (10 minutes) for a command, 900 (15 minutes) for an agent, 1200 (20 minutes) for a build and 900 (15 minutes) for CI. The guard also accepts a background launch with a timeout up to 1,200,000 ms (20 minutes). waitfor.py checks each minute, but a build can still run for 20 minutes before anyone learns it failed. Tests: another session on your other account designed modular tests (docs/4-systems/modular-tests.md, issues 575 to 582, approved 2026-11-23, not built). It gives each test module a name and a command to run it alone, adds a runner that takes a --parts option, and includes a conversion skill that proves the old and new runs report the same checks. It covers tests only, not builds, installs, renders or agent runs. I ran the whole of verify.py on this branch: core 68.9 seconds, safe_git 127.6 seconds, design_loop 201.1 seconds, writing 8.5 seconds, delegation 142.9 seconds, docs 46.7 seconds and make_page 105.5 seconds. Five of the seven parts took over a minute, and the slowest, design_loop, took over three minutes (201.1 seconds). That run also had failures (1 failure in core, 3 in safe_git, 3 in delegation, 1 in make_page; design_loop stopped without printing a result line). This branch changes four documentation files and no plugin code, and the same checks pass on main's continuous-integration run (automated checks on GitHub; 1 minute 22 seconds, on Linux). So the failures come from running on this Windows machine, not from this work; fixing them is a separate item.
A 60-second foreground limit, 20-minute background deadlines, modular tests designed but not built.
One segment rule for all wait-bound work, with tests as the first case.
You wait about a minute per part, and a failure stops the run early.
new
The segment plan, written before any long job starts
Before waiting on anything, the model writes a plan of segments, each with its own deadline.

The existing wait statement already names what is awaited, how it is checked, what done means, and the deadline. The statement becomes a short table with one row per segment: segment name, the one command, the input it needs and how that input is checked (a check that takes seconds), the output it leaves, and the 60-second deadline. The model starts segment 1, reads its result, and only then starts segment 2. If a segment fails, the later ones are not started, and the reply names the failed segment and shows its output. The plan is the one place that says how the work is cut up, so tests, builds, installs, renders and agent runs all follow the same rule. I would add this section to rules/detail/waits.md.
A wait states its deadline but not how the work is cut up.
A segment table before every job over a minute.
Failures are caught at the first segment that fails.
new
Addition 1: a 60-second limit on every wait
Any segment, test module or run that takes over a minute is flagged and must be split.

For tests, the module header gains a measured time recorded after each run, and the gate (issue 578) and audit (issue 579) flag every module over 60 seconds with its name and time. For all other work, rules/waits.json lowers the 600, 900 and 1200 second deadlines (10, 15 and 20 minutes) to 60 seconds per segment, and the guard refuses a background launch whose timeout is over 60,000 ms unless the launch description contains "Cannot split:" followed by a reason, the same way the guard already accepts "no safe way:". A job that truly cannot split, such as a CI run or one engine build, may stay whole, but it must report progress at least every minute, so waitfor.py can show one result per minute. The 60 is read from rules/waits.json, so it changes in one place.
Foreground limit 60 seconds; background up to 20 minutes.
60 seconds per segment everywhere; a named exit for the rare job that cannot split.
A slow job is split before it starts, not after you have waited.
adapt
Addition 2: each segment prints its own result, as it finishes
Results appear per segment, in the order they finish.

Every segment ends with its own PASS or FAIL line and a final RESULT line, in the same format verify.py already prints. For tests, the gate requires this in the module header. verify.py itself has to change. Today it prints the parts in a fixed order, so a finished part waits behind a slower one before its result shows. The change makes it print each part the moment that part finishes. For other work, the segment plan lists each segment's result line, so the model reads one result per minute and stops at the first segment that prints FAIL.
verify.py holds finished output until earlier parts end.
Each module prints when done.
You and the model see results sooner.
new
Addition 3: segments that stand alone, not chained together
Each segment runs alone, so one failure never hides behind another.

A segment has one command, one named input and one named output. Its input is a named file or a freshly created state, and the segment checks it at the very start, so a missing input fails in seconds. The input is never something left behind in memory or on disk by the previous segment's process. A job with a real data flow, such as compile then link then package, passes each output to the next as a named checkpoint file, so any segment can be re-run alone without the earlier ones. For tests, the conversion skill runs each module alone and then all in shuffled order and compares; a mismatch is reported as a hidden dependency between modules, and the skill does not try to fix it. For other work, the plan states each segment's input check and the test is to run that segment alone once.
The proof compares counts only.
Each segment checked alone, and tests also shuffled.
A hidden dependency is caught the first time, not after a 20-minute run.
risk
Flaws I found in this design
Four known gaps, each with its answer.

One: the stricter, written judge could still disagree with the scripted record check. Both read the same criteria text and the same method classes, so they cannot differ on what counts. Two: a model could write fake methods, so the record is checked against real failed tool calls. Three: a shared cap of two with no reset would leave a long unattended run unchecked after the first two blocks, so the cap resets after real tool work. Four: I have not confirmed whether Claude Code's own limit of 8 consecutive blocks applies to prompt hooks. The missing cap does not explain the 12 blocks, so the build plan adds a replay of a real session to find out why.
None of these gaps is handled today.
Each gap has a test or a stated limit.
You see the limits before approving.
risk
Flaws I found in the segment design
Five known gaps, each with its answer.

One: speed differs by machine, so the time is measured and recorded on the machine that runs the work, not assumed. Two: a split can hide a real dependency; running each module alone and then in shuffled order is the proof for tests, and the input check is the proof for other work. Three: one engine build, install or CI run may never fit in 60 seconds; the Cannot split line is the exit, and such a job must still report progress each minute, otherwise a check every minute shows nothing, and the failure is found late anyway. Four: the 12-block loop came from a judge, so every new refusal in this design needs the shared cap of two blocks and a copyable accepted reply. Without both, the new refusals could loop the same way. Five: refusing a long background launch could block a legitimate job; the one-line "Cannot split:" exit is the answer, and each use is logged so I can see how often it happens.
Nothing guards against these today.
Each gap has a test or a stated limit.
You see the limits before approving.
choices: first
Where should the judge run, so that it can see the attempts and keep a count of its blocks?
A
Move it into the scripted Stop hook, which would call the Haiku model from inside the script, the way the goal check already does
The judge can read the real tool calls, share the counter, and return the criterion that failed. It adds up to 22 seconds, but only when a claim is flagged.
B
Leave it as the prompt hook; add the written criteria, and let the reply pass on the retry
This is the smallest change, but the judge still cannot see the tool calls or keep a count, so it can still wrongly block a model that did the work.
The judge has to see the real attempts to be fair, and only a script can both see them and keep a count of blocks.
share
What should the shared cap be?
A
Two blocks, reset after real tool work
Matches today's record check. The blocks are limited, but long unattended runs are still checked.
B
Two blocks per user message, no reset
Simplest, but an unattended run is no longer checked after two blocks.
C
Three blocks
One more block per reply, so the loop could run one step longer.
A cap of two with a reset ends the loop and still checks long unattended runs.
flask
How strictly should the 60-second rule be enforced for work that is not a test?
A
Refuse a background launch with a timeout over 60 seconds, unless its description says "Cannot split:" and gives the reason
It stops a 20-minute wait before it starts, and the way out is a single line, so the refusal cannot loop.
B
Only warn, and print the segment plan without refusing the launch
Nothing stops a long wait from being started again.
C
Enforce the limit only for builds and installs
Leaves agent runs and renders open.
Refusing at launch is the only point where the limit holds, because a hook cannot interrupt a wait that has already begun.
share
How should a job where each step needs the previous step's output, such as compile then link then package, be handled?
A
Pass each output on as a named checkpoint file (a saved file the next segment reads), and have the next segment check it at its start
Every segment can be re-run alone, and a missing input fails in seconds.
B
Forbid any dependency between segments
Too strict, because some work cannot be done without a dependency.
A checkpoint file keeps each segment independent while allowing real data to flow.

wrapup.summary: A proposal with two linked parts: stop the end-of-reply judge looping, and cut every wait-bound job, tests included, into independent segments of at most a minute.
wrapup.changing: Nothing is built. It would edit hooks.json, scripts/house_rules/core.py, rules/detail/roadblocks.md, rules/waits.json, rules/detail/waits.md, the launch guard and verify.py, and extend the approved modular-tests design (issues 575 to 582).
wrapup.blocking: Your approval and your four choices: where the judge runs, the shared cap, how hard the 60-second rule is enforced for non-test work, and how a data flow between segments is handled.
wrapup.next: After you approve, I record the decision, create one parent issue with a child issue per part, write a build plan, and start with the judge criteria and a replay of 12 blocked replies as a verify.py case.
